lessons.0.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 1 - 20 minutes
lessons.0.slides.0.description: Learn a systematic approach to tasting
lessons.0.slides.1.title: The Three Stages of Tasting
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Professional tasting proceeds through visual, olfactory, and gustatory stages. Each stage reveals different information about the wine. A systematic approach enables accurate assessment of quality, origin, age, and ageing potential.
lessons.0.slides.2.title: 👁️ Visual Examination
lessons.0.slides.2.points.0: Colour depth — young vs. aged, variety, level of extraction
lessons.0.slides.2.points.2: Whites: pale yellow-green → golden → amber → brown
lessons.0.slides.2.points.3: Clarity — clear vs. cloudy (may indicate sediment)
lessons.0.slides.2.points.4: Viscosity — 'legs' or 'tears' indicate alcohol and glycerol
lessons.0.slides.3.title: 👃 Olfactory Analysis
lessons.0.slides.3.points.0: First nose — still wine, capturing initial aromas
lessons.0.slides.3.points.1: Second nose — after swirling, releasing more aromas
lessons.0.slides.3.points.2: Intensity — closed vs. open vs. expressive
lessons.0.slides.3.points.4: Aroma types — fruit, floral, spice, mineral, etc.
lessons.0.slides.3.points.5: Fault check — cork taint, oxidation, reduction
lessons.0.slides.3.points.6: Evolution — how aromas change over time
lessons.0.slides.4.title: 👅 Gustatory Tasting
lessons.0.slides.4.points.0: First sip — overall impression and balance
lessons.0.slides.4.points.1: Acidity — lively, fresh, sharp, or flat
lessons.0.slides.4.points.2: Tannins — firm, silky, or coarse (reds only)
lessons.0.slides.4.points.4: Alcohol — warm sensation, balanced vs. burning
lessons.0.slides.4.points.7: Evolution — how it develops from entry → mid-palate → finish
lessons.0.slides.5.title: 📝 Tasting Note Essentials
lessons.0.slides.5.points.0: Basic information: wine name, vintage, producer, serving temperature
lessons.0.slides.5.points.2: Aromas: intensity, complexity, specific aroma descriptions
lessons.0.slides.5.points.3: Palate: acidity, tannins, body, alcohol, balance
lessons.0.slides.5.points.5: Overall assessment: quality score, drinking window, ageing potential
lessons.0.slides.6.title: Young vs. Aged Wine Tasting Differences

lessons.1.title: Aroma Identification and Classification
lessons.1.slides.0.title: Aroma Identification
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 2 - 22 minutes
lessons.1.slides.0.description: Learn to identify the typical aromas of Burgundy wines
lessons.1.slides.1.title: The Three Levels of Aroma
lessons.1.slides.1.content: Primary aromas come from the grape variety itself; secondary aromas from the fermentation process; tertiary aromas (bouquet) from bottle ageing. Burgundy's charm lies in the perfect integration of all three levels.
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 🌺 Aroma Classification System
lessons.1.slides.2.points.2: Tertiary (bouquet): leather, forest floor, animal, spice
lessons.1.slides.2.points.5: Tip: identify the source of each aroma category
lessons.1.slides.3.title: 🍇 Typical Pinot Noir Aromas
lessons.1.slides.3.points.0: Red fruit: cherry, strawberry, raspberry, cranberry
lessons.1.slides.3.points.4: Forest: mushroom, truffle, wet earth, fallen leaves
lessons.1.slides.3.points.5: With age: animal leather, smoke, humus
lessons.1.slides.3.points.6: Different villages display different aromatic signatures
lessons.1.slides.4.title: 🌸 Pinot Noir Aroma Wheel
lessons.1.slides.4.content: Typical aroma categories and evolution of Burgundy Pinot Noir
lessons.1.slides.5.title: 🥂 Typical Chardonnay Aromas
lessons.1.slides.5.points.1: White fruit: apple, pear, white peach
lessons.1.slides.5.points.5: Mineral: flint, wet stone, ocean notes
lessons.1.slides.5.points.6: With age: honey, butter, toasted bread
lessons.1.slides.6.title: 🏔️ Regional Aromatic Signatures
lessons.1.slides.6.points.0: Chablis: flint, oyster shell, lemon, mineral
lessons.1.slides.6.points.1: Côte de Nuits: black fruit, forest, animal leather
lessons.1.slides.6.points.2: Côte de Beaune whites: hazelnut, butter, white blossom, mineral
lessons.1.slides.6.points.3: Côte de Beaune reds: red fruit, florals, elegant spice
lessons.1.slides.7.title: ⚠️ Identifying Fault Aromas
lessons.1.slides.7.points.1: Oxidation — sherry-like, caramel, loss of fruit
lessons.1.slides.7.points.2: Reduction — rotten eggs, rubber, struck match
lessons.1.slides.7.points.6: Fault recognition is an essential tasting skill
lessons.1.slides.8.title: How to Train Your Nose
lessons.1.slides.8.content: Build an aroma memory bank: smell real ingredients (fresh cherries, roses etc.); use aroma kits; practise blind tasting; keep tasting notes; compare the same variety from different appellations; taste regularly to sharpen olfactory sensitivity.
lessons.1.slides.9.title: 🎯 Practical Tasting Tips
lessons.1.slides.9.points.1: Decanting: young wines 1–2 hours, aged wines 30 minutes
lessons.1.slides.9.points.2: Glass choice: large-bowled, narrow-mouthed Burgundy glass
lessons.1.slides.9.points.3: Swirling technique: gentle rotation to release aromas
lessons.1.slides.9.points.5: Tasting order: light to heavy, whites before reds
lessons.1.slides.9.points.6: Blind tasting: the most effective way to learn

lessons.2.title: Structure Analysis and Balance
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Structure and Balance
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 3 - 18 minutes
lessons.2.slides.0.description: Understand the structural components of wine and how to assess balance
lessons.2.slides.1.title: What Is Wine Structure?
lessons.2.slides.1.content: Structure refers to the skeleton that supports a wine, built from acidity, tannins (red wine), alcohol, and fruit. The key to fine Burgundy lies in the perfect balance of these elements.
lessons.2.slides.2.title: ⚖️ Balance Elements in Red Wine
lessons.2.slides.2.points.0: Acidity — provides freshness and ageing potential
lessons.2.slides.2.points.4: Perfect balance: all four elements support each other, none dominating
lessons.2.slides.2.points.5: Burgundy signature: high acidity, fine tannins, moderate alcohol
lessons.2.slides.3.title: 🥂 Balance Elements in White Wine
lessons.2.slides.3.points.3: Residual sugar (minimal) — Burgundy whites are almost entirely dry
lessons.2.slides.3.points.5: Ideal: vibrant acidity + rich flavour + elegant texture
lessons.2.slides.4.title: 📊 How to Assess Balance
lessons.2.slides.4.points.0: Too much acidity — sharp, lacking fruit
lessons.2.slides.4.points.1: Too little acidity — flat, heavy, not refreshing
lessons.2.slides.4.points.2: Too much tannin — astringent, coarse, hard to drink
lessons.2.slides.4.points.3: Too little tannin — lacking structure, overly soft
lessons.2.slides.4.points.4: Too much alcohol — burning sensation, loss of elegance
lessons.2.slides.4.points.5: Too little alcohol — thin, lacking body
lessons.2.slides.4.points.6: Perfect balance: tasting reveals no single component standing out
lessons.2.slides.5.title: Young vs. Aged Wine Balance
lessons.2.slides.6.title: The Importance of Texture
lessons.2.slides.6.content: The hallmark of top Burgundy is 'silky texture'. Reds: tannins as fine as velvet, smooth on entry. Whites: creamy smoothness that retains freshness. Texture reveals terroir and winemaking mastery more than fruit flavour alone.

lessons.3.title: Assessing Ageing Potential
lessons.3.slides.0.title: Assessing Ageing Potential
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 4 - 15 minutes
lessons.3.slides.0.description: Learn to evaluate a wine's capacity to age
lessons.3.slides.1.title: 🕰️ Factors Determining Ageing Potential
lessons.3.slides.1.points.0: Acidity — the most critical factor; high acidity = long ageing
lessons.3.slides.1.points.1: Tannins (reds) — firm, fine tannins preserve well over time
lessons.3.slides.1.points.2: Concentration — extract-rich wines are more durable
lessons.3.slides.1.points.3: Balance — a balanced wine remains balanced with age
lessons.3.slides.1.points.4: Vintage — great vintages have longer ageing trajectories
lessons.3.slides.1.points.5: Terroir — Grand Cru > Premier Cru > Village
lessons.3.slides.1.points.6: Winemaking — traditional methods age better than modern
lessons.3.slides.2.title: 📅 Ageing Guidelines by Classification
lessons.3.slides.2.points.7: Beaujolais Nouveau: drink in the current year
lessons.3.slides.3.title: Ageing Curve of Top Burgundy
lessons.3.slides.4.title: 🔍 Judging Ageing Potential from Tasting
lessons.3.slides.4.points.0: Closed when young — aromas not open = needs time
lessons.3.slides.4.points.1: Firm tannins — if quality is good = has potential
lessons.3.slides.4.points.2: Lively acidity — stimulating but not sharp = will soften
lessons.3.slides.4.points.3: Concentrated fruit — sufficient to support long ageing
lessons.3.slides.4.points.4: Long finish — extended finish = high quality = ageworthy
lessons.3.slides.4.points.6: Complexity — already showing layers = will improve further
lessons.3.slides.5.title: ⚠️ Assessing the Drinking Window
lessons.3.slides.5.points.3: Plateau — holds quality without further development
lessons.3.slides.5.points.4: Decline — fruit fading, oxidative notes appearing
lessons.3.slides.5.points.6: Great vintages age longer than difficult ones
lessons.3.slides.6.title: Collecting and Drinking Strategy
lessons.3.slides.6.content: Buy young wines: purchase at least 6 bottles, open one every 2–3 years to track evolution. Top wines: age at least 10 years before opening the first bottle. Premier Cru: start tasting after 5–8 years. Village wine: ready after 3–5 years. Keep tasting notes to track development.
lessons.3.slides.7.title: 📊 Effect of Storage Conditions on Ageing
lessons.3.slides.7.points.1: Humidity: 70–75%, to prevent corks drying and cracking
lessons.3.slides.7.points.2: Light: avoid direct light; total darkness is best
lessons.3.slides.7.points.4: Position: lay horizontally to keep cork moist
lessons.3.slides.7.points.5: Air: ventilated but free of odours
lessons.3.slides.7.points.6: Perfect conditions can extend wine's life by 30–50%
lessons.3.slides.8.title: 🧠 Ageing Potential Assessment Quiz
